title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
summary: Girl with a Pearl Earring is an oil painting by Dutch Golden Age painter Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it acquired its present title towards the end of the 20th century. The work has been in the collection of the Mauritshuis in The Hague since 1902 and has been the subject of various literary and cinematic treatments.

sections.name: her face
sections.description: The subject's enigmatic gaze and slightly parted lips create a sense of intimacy and mystery. Her pale skin and subtle features are softly illuminated against the dark background.

sections.name: the pearl earring
sections.description: The focal point of the piece, this large pearl earring is rendered with just a few highlights. It symbolizes wealth and adds a brilliant touch of light to the shadowed side of her face.

sections.name: the turban
sections.description: The exotic blue turban is painted using expensive ultramarine pigment, indicating her unique attire. Its folds and wrap around her head give the composition a sense of volume.

sections.name: her jacket
sections.description: Her simple brownish-yellow garment has a modest white collar, providing a grounded contrast to the elaborate headgear. The textures of the fabric are captured through soft brushwork.

museum_facts: The Mauritshuis dates the painting to around 1665 and says it is on view in Room 15.
It is not a portrait of a known person but a “tronie,” a study of an imaginary figure in exotic dress.
Vermeer used soft transitions to model the girl’s face, while small dabs of paint suggest reflected light on her clothing.
The oversized pearl is probably an imitation: Vermeer suggested it with just two brushstrokes, and painted no silver hook.

guide_notes.her face: Your fingertips are resting on the smooth oval of the girl's face at the center of the relief, tilted over her shoulder toward you, with a raised ridge along its upper edge where the headdress begins. This is the least textured part of the whole plate: a gently domed surface with no sharp edges except the small ridge of the nose and the shallow recess where the lips part. Trace down one side to find the softly raised cheek and the slightly sunken corner of the mouth, then across to the eye sockets, which are only faint hollows rather than carved detail. Long thought to have no eyelashes at all, the face was shown in the 2018-2020 'Girl in the Spotlight' study to have tiny individual hairs painted around both eyes, invisible to the naked eye and revealed only through macro X-ray fluorescence scanning.
guide_notes.the pearl earring: Just below the jaw and to one side of the face, your fingers will find a single smooth teardrop hanging free of the relief, its surface the most polished and glossy point on the entire plate. It sits low near the collar, with a raised dab of highlight at the top and a flat, smooth lower curve that rests against the background. Nothing connects it upward to the ear, so there is no hook or loop to trace. That missing link is exactly what curators point out: the 'pearl' is an illusion with no contour and no hook to hang from, and during the 1994 restoration a smaller second highlight on its surface turned out to be a flake of loosened paint that had flipped onto the canvas, removed so the drop shows only the single highlight Vermeer intended.
guide_notes.the turban: Rising above the face, the headdress is a broad wrapped band your fingers can follow all the way around the crown, with a wide pale-yellow fold at the front crossing over a deeper blue section at the side. The two materials meet in a raised seam just above the forehead, and the blue area feels flatter and drier than the glossier white collar far below it. Follow the yellow band around and you can feel where it twists and tucks behind the head, ending the head shape at the top of the plate. The blue part was painted with natural ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan, a costly pigment Vermeer used here more freely than most of his contemporaries, and the resulting turban is so unusual that art historians have found no clear parallel for it in European painting.
guide_notes.her jacket: Below the face and the narrow white band at the throat, the relief drops into the broad, gently curving plane of the girl's jacket, sloping outward toward the lower edge of the plate. Your fingers can feel a crisp, raised white collar at the top, worked in noticeably thicker paint than the smooth ochre fabric beneath it, while the jacket itself is a soft, unbroken surface with only the shallowest hint of a fold. It runs off the bottom edge without arms or hands, so the plate stops at the upper mass of the garment. Vermeer built this area in a strict order, painting the background first, then the face, then the yellow jacket, and only afterward the white collar, the headscarf and finally the 'pearl', and the collar's thick impasto stands out from the drier jacket as one of the clearest material contrasts on the canvas.
